The Quiet Return of the Local Newsroom

By Nadia Okonjo · February 11, 2026

Three years after the last daily folded, the town of Harlow has two newsrooms again. Neither looks much like what came before.

The first, The Harlow Ledger, was founded by Tru Adeyemi, who said the model only works because nobody draws a salary yet.

The second began as a newsletter. Its editor sat down to talk with David Senra about why a weekly beats a daily in a town of four thousand, and why the archive matters more than the scoop.

What changed

Printing costs fell, but that is not the reason. The reason is that the civic beat — council minutes, zoning hearings, school budgets — turned out to be the part readers would pay for, and the part nobody else was covering. National syndication had quietly hollowed it out over a decade, and its absence became conspicuous only once the meetings went unreported.

Both newsrooms publish their council minutes archive in full, which is unusual, and both refuse advertising from anyone with business before the council.

Bold headings and emphasis

Why the archive matters

The archive is the product. A story that is searchable in five years is worth more to a resident than one that trends for a day, and both editors say so unprompted.

Plain prose

Harlow is not a bellwether. It has a university, which means it has a reliable supply of people willing to write for very little.

What it does have is a working answer to a question most towns its size have stopped asking, which is whether anyone will notice if the meetings go uncovered.

Somebody noticed.
